etymology: From Old English lufu, affection, rendering Hebrew ahabah and Greek agape; the settled, willing good of God toward His creatures and, peculiarly, toward His elect.
biblical_def: The love of God is His eternal, self-moved goodness, by which He wills and works the good of His creatures, and most of all the everlasting salvation of His elect. We must distinguish His general benevolence, by which He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and the good (Matt 5:45), from His special, electing, saving love set upon His people before the foundation of the world. This saving love is not occasioned by anything lovely in us, for "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8). It is electing love: "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world" (Eph 1:4-5). It is redeeming love: "In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him" (1 John 4:9). And it is propitiating love, for herein is love, that He sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). This love is no soft sentimentalism that overlooks sin; it is holy love that satisfies justice at the cross. This dictionary confesses that the love of God is sovereign, particular, and unbreakable, the fountain of election and the ground of all our hope.
webster_summary: The love of God is His self-moved goodness toward His creatures, and chiefly His electing, redeeming affection set upon the elect. It is distinguished from mere benevolence to all by its saving particularity. It is holy, not sentimental, satisfying justice at the cross.
webster_full: LOVE OF GOD, noun. The eternal and gracious disposition of God to will and work the good of His creatures, and supremely the salvation of His elect.
It is distinguished into a general benevolence shown to all, and a special saving love set upon His chosen.
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8).
It requires that we love Him in return with heart, soul, mind, and strength; it forbids that we mistake His love for indulgence of sin.
It is the spring of election, the gift of the Son, and the seal of an everlasting covenant that cannot fail.
scriptures: John 3:16
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Rom 5:8
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will.
1 John 4:9
In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him.
corruption_summary: The age recasts the love of God as an unconditional, undiscriminating affirmation that never judges and never condemns, severing love from holiness and wrath.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion loves to say "God is love" while emptying the word of its biblical content. It makes divine love a blanket approval of every man as he is, a love that demands no repentance and tolerates every sin, so that hell becomes unthinkable and the cross becomes unnecessary. But Scripture binds love to holiness: the same God who is love is also a consuming fire, and His love for the elect was purchased by the pouring out of His wrath upon His Son. A love that will not satisfy justice is not the love of the living God but an idol of sentiment.

Recover the holy, electing, particular love that runs through the covenant of grace. God set His love upon a people, gave His Son to die for them, and will bring every one of them home. This love is tender beyond telling, yet it never winks at sin; it slays sin at the cross that the beloved may be made holy. To know oneself loved with such love is the strongest motive to godliness and the surest comfort in affliction.
roots_summary: Behind love lie Hebrew ahabah and Greek agape, the willing, self-giving good of God toward His people.
roots_lines: Hebrew ahabah, love, is rooted in covenant choice, as the LORD loved Israel not for her greatness (Deut 7:7-8).
Greek agape denotes a deliberate, self-giving good will, supremely shown in the gift of the Son.
The verb agapao in John 3:16 governs the giving of the only begotten Son for sinners.
Old English lufu supplies our word love, but Scripture fills it with electing and redeeming content.
The summit of the word is 1 John 4:10, where love is defined by propitiation, not by sentiment.
usage: The love of God in election is the deep spring from which every mercy in our salvation flows.
He warned them never to set the love of God against the wrath of God, for both meet at the cross.
Her dying comfort was the love of God, sealed in the blood of the everlasting covenant.

etymology: From offer, Latin offerre, to present or hold forth; the gracious presenting of Christ to all who hear the gospel, with a sincere call to come.
biblical_def: The free offer of the gospel is the well-meant proclamation in which Christ, with all His benefits, is sincerely held forth to every hearer, with a true command to repent and believe and a genuine promise of salvation to all who come. The offer is universal in its proclamation, though redemption is particular in its accomplishment. God calls indiscriminately: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters" (Isa 55:1), and Christ Himself cries, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28). The Spirit and the bride say, "Come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Rev 22:17). This sincere call stands in full harmony with particular redemption, for the offer is to be made to all, while the saving power of it belongs to the elect through effectual calling. Against the cold error of hyper-Calvinism, which forbids the free offer and will not press Christ upon sinners, this dictionary confesses that the gospel is to be preached to every creature, that God is not the author of any man's ruin, and that the warrant to believe rests not on secret election but on the open command and promise of God in the gospel.
webster_summary: The free offer is the sincere holding-forth of Christ to every hearer, with a true command to believe and a real promise to all who come. It is consistent with particular redemption, for the offer is universal while saving power is the elect's. It is denied by hyper-Calvinism, which this dictionary rejects.
webster_full: FREE OFFER, noun. The sincere and well-meant presentation of Christ and His salvation to all who hear the gospel.
It includes a genuine command to repent and believe and a real promise of life to all who come.
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).
It requires the preacher to press Christ upon every sinner; it forbids the withholding of the gospel from any.
It stands consistent with definite atonement, the offer being universal and the saving call effectual in the elect.
scriptures: Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Matt 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
Ezek 33:11

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
corruption_summary: Two errors flank the truth: hyper-Calvinism denies the well-meant offer, while Arminianism grounds it in a universal atonement and the autonomous free will of man.
corruption_paragraphs: Hyper-Calvinism, fearing to compromise sovereignty, refuses to offer Christ to all and will only address the offer to sensible sinners or the awakened. This chills evangelism, hides the warrant to believe, and contradicts the apostolic pattern of preaching repentance to every creature. On the opposite hand, Arminianism makes the offer rest on a universal redemption and a will free to turn itself, so that the decisive cause of salvation lies in the sinner. Both miss the biblical balance.

Scripture holds the offer and the decree together without strain. God sincerely commands all to come and truly promises life to all who do, while the effectual call savingly draws the elect. The preacher is to spread the table wide and beseech men to be reconciled to God; the secret election is the Lord's business, the open offer is ours. This is the apostolic temper, and the church neglects it to her own coldness.
roots_summary: The offer is rooted in the gospel imperatives of Scripture, where Christ is held forth and sinners are commanded to come.
roots_lines: The Hebrew imperative of Isa 55:1, leku, "come ye," opens the invitation to all the thirsty.
The Greek deute in Matt 11:28, "come," is Christ's own summons to the heavy-laden.
The word offer, from Latin offerre, means to hold forth or present freely.
The phrase "whosoever will" in Rev 22:17 marks the universal sweep of the gospel call.
Ezek 33:11 grounds the sincerity of the call in God's declared pleasure that the wicked turn and live.
usage: He pressed the free offer upon every soul in the room, beseeching them to come to Christ at once.
The free offer of the gospel and the doctrine of particular redemption are not enemies but companions.
Hyper-Calvinism silenced the free offer in that pulpit, and the congregation grew cold and small.

etymology: From Old English wisdom, the quality of being wise; rendering Hebrew chokmah and Greek sophia, the skill of living rightly before God.
biblical_def: Wisdom in Scripture is not bare knowledge nor worldly cleverness, but the God-given skill of ordering all of life in the fear of the LORD. Its beginning and first principle is reverence toward God: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (Prov 1:7), and again, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding" (Prov 9:10). Hebrew chokmah denotes a practical mastery, the craftsman's skill applied to the whole craft of godly living, so that the wise man walks in the paths of righteousness and shuns the way of the fool. This wisdom is finally a Person, for Christ "of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 1:30); to have Him is to have wisdom itself, and the cross which the world calls foolishness is the very wisdom of God. The wisdom from above is also a moral character: "first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated" (Jas 3:17). This dictionary confesses that true wisdom is not the boast of the learned nor the shrewdness of the worldly, but the fear of God worked by His Spirit, found and treasured in Christ, and shown forth in a holy and useful life.
webster_summary: Wisdom is the God-given skill of living rightly, beginning in the fear of the LORD. It is found supremely in Christ, who is made unto us wisdom. It is practical godliness, not mere intellect or worldly cleverness.
webster_full: WISDOM, noun. The God-given skill of ordering one's life and affairs rightly in the fear of the LORD.
It is distinguished from mere knowledge, cleverness, or the wisdom of this world, which God brings to nought.
"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding" (Prov 9:10).
It requires reverence, obedience, and the choosing of righteousness; it forbids the folly that despises instruction.
Its fulness and treasury is Christ, who is made unto us wisdom from God.
scriptures: Prov 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Prov 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.
Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
corruption_summary: The age severs wisdom from the fear of God, making it a self-derived cleverness, technique, or inner intuition rather than reverent, obedient skill in living.
corruption_paragraphs: The world prizes a wisdom that begins not in the fear of God but in self, whether the academic shrewdness of the learned or the soft "inner wisdom" of the therapeutic age that tells men to trust their hearts. But Scripture calls the heart deceitful, and the wisdom of this world foolishness with God. To divorce wisdom from reverence is to build skill upon sand, however polished the result may appear.

Recover the biblical order: the fear of the LORD first, then knowledge, then a life skillfully built in righteousness. Such wisdom is humble, teachable, and finally Christological, for all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in Christ. The believer grows wise not by climbing into himself but by bowing before God and feeding on His word.
roots_summary: Wisdom renders Hebrew chokmah, skill, and Greek sophia, both anchored in the fear of the LORD.
roots_lines: Hebrew chokmah first describes the skill of artisans (Exod 31:3) before naming the skill of godly living.
Greek sophia in 1 Cor 1:30 is fulfilled in Christ, in whom wisdom is incarnate.
The recurring formula "the fear of the LORD" (Prov 1:7; 9:10) names wisdom's beginning and principle.
Old English wisdom joins wis, wise, to the suffix denoting state or quality.
James 3:17 supplies the moral marks of the wisdom from above, pure and peaceable.
usage: He sought wisdom not in cleverness but in the fear of the LORD, where Scripture says it begins.
True wisdom is found in Christ, who of God is made unto us wisdom and righteousness.
The young man mistook worldly cleverness for wisdom and stumbled into the way of the fool.

etymology: From the Pauline phrase heis en Christo (Gal 3:28), one in Christ; the gospel unity of all believers in the one body of the Lord.
biblical_def: To be one in Christ is to share, with all the redeemed, a common standing and a common life in the Lord Jesus, by whom the ancient division between Jew and Gentile is abolished. Paul declares, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). Christ "is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us" (Eph 2:14), reconciling Jew and Gentile in one body unto God by the cross (Eph 2:16). This unity is real, deep, and gracious: every believer, whatever his nation or station, is justified by the same faith, indwelt by the same Spirit, and an heir of the same promise. Yet this oneness in Christ does NOT erase the creational order God established before the fall. Galatians speaks of equal standing in justification, not the abolition of sex or office; the same apostle who wrote "neither male nor female" also ordered male-only eldership and creational headship in the home and the church. The progressive reading that presses Gal 3:28 to dissolve the two sexes, to ordain women, or to bless same-sex unions twists a text about gospel access into a charter for autonomy. This dictionary confesses that all believers are gloriously one in Christ, while the distinctions of sex and office that God wove into creation abide.
webster_summary: To be one in Christ is to share a common standing and life in the Lord, Jew and Gentile reconciled in one body. The middle wall of partition is broken down by the cross. This unity does not erase the creational order of sex and office.
webster_full: ONE IN CHRIST, noun phrase. The gospel unity of all believers, joined in one body by their common standing in the Lord Jesus.
It abolishes the old division between Jew and Gentile and levels every distinction of nation or station before the cross.
"There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28).
It requires brotherly love and equal honor among the saints; it forbids the partitions of pride that the world raises.
It concerns equal standing in justification, not the dissolving of the creational order of sex and office.
scriptures: Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us.
Eph 2:16
And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby.
Col 3:11
Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all.
corruption_summary: The progressive movement seizes Galatians 3:28 to abolish the creational distinctions of sex and office, turning a text about gospel access into a charter for women's ordination, gender ideology, and affirming sexuality.
corruption_paragraphs: Affirming and egalitarian teachers read "neither male nor female" as though Paul had erased the two sexes God made in creation, and so they ordain women to the eldership, baptize transgender self-definition, and bless same-sex unions in the name of inclusion. But the apostle is plainly speaking of equal access to justifying grace, for Jew and Gentile, slave and free, man and woman alike are heirs of Abraham by faith. The very letters that proclaim this oneness also command wives to submit, restrict the eldership to qualified men, and root these orders in creation, not culture. To pit Galatians 3 against 1 Timothy 2 is to set the Spirit against Himself.

Recover the true and glorious unity: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one body in which the wall between the nations is forever down. This unity does not flatten the good order God wove into our creation as male and female, nor the offices He appointed in His church. Equal standing before God and distinct callings within His order are both gifts of the same wise Lord, and the church flourishes when she holds them together.
roots_summary: The phrase grows from Paul's heis en Christo and the image of the broken middle wall of partition.
roots_lines: Greek heis, one, in Gal 3:28 stresses a single shared standing, not a single undifferentiated mass.
The phrase en Christo, in Christ, names the union by which believers share His life and benefits.
Greek mesotoichon, the "middle wall" of Eph 2:14, pictures the temple barrier between Jew and Gentile.
The context of Gal 3 is sonship and inheritance by faith, defining the kind of oneness in view.
Col 3:11 parallels the list, climaxing in "Christ is all, and in all," the center of the union.
usage: Being one in Christ, the freed slave and his former master sat at the same Table as brothers.
He cherished the oneness believers have in Christ without ever pretending it dissolved the offices of the church.
The teacher abused "neither male nor female" to ordain women, mistaking gospel access for the erasure of order.

etymology: From Hebrew eben ha-ezer, the stone of help (1 Sam 7:12); help from Old English help, succor or aid rendered in need.
biblical_def: The help of God is His timely and effectual succor of His people in their need, the strong arm by which He upholds, delivers, and sustains those who call upon Him. When the LORD had routed the Philistines, "Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Eben-ezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us" (1 Sam 7:12). The stone was a memorial, a heaped witness that all the way thus far was paved with mercy. The psalmist makes this help a refuge in calamity: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Psa 46:1), and again, "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth" (Psa 121:2). Such help is not a vague optimism but the concrete intervention of a covenant God who hears, defends, and provides. The remembrance of past mercies is itself a means of grace, for the saint who counts up his Ebenezers is fortified against present fear and future doubt. This dictionary confesses that the people of God are kept not by their own strength but by His ready help, and that gratitude for mercies received is the proper soil of faith for mercies yet to come.
webster_summary: The help of God is His timely succor of His people, memorialized in Samuel's stone Ebenezer. He is a very present help in trouble. The remembrance of past mercies strengthens faith for the future.
webster_full: HELP OF GOD, noun. The effectual aid and succor God renders His people in their time of need.
It was memorialized by Samuel in the stone Ebenezer, a witness that the LORD had helped His people thus far.
"God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Psa 46:1).
It requires that we call upon Him and remember His mercies; it forbids the self-reliance that forgets the Giver.
It is the ground of confidence that He who has helped will help still, even unto the end.
scriptures: Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Eben-ezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
Psa 46:1
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
Heb 13:6
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
corruption_summary: The age trades the help of a personal, covenant God for self-help, positive thinking, and the autonomous self as its own savior.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the spirit of the age quietly replaces the help of God with the gospel of self-reliance, where a man looks within for strength and counts his deliverances as the fruit of his own resolve. Such pride forgets the Giver and leaves the soul without refuge when its own strength fails.

Recover the practice of the Ebenezer: heap up the memorials of mercy and say with Samuel, "Hitherto hath the LORD helped us." The saint who remembers past help is armed against present fear, for the God who has been a very present help in trouble does not change. Gratitude looks back upon mercy and so looks forward with faith.
roots_summary: The word Ebenezer joins Hebrew eben, stone, to ezer, help, naming the LORD as the helper of His people.
roots_lines: Hebrew eben, stone, supplies the first half of Ebenezer, the memorial Samuel raised.
Hebrew ezer, help, is the same word used of the help God Himself supplies in Psa 121:2.
The clause ad-hennah, "hitherto," marks the backward look over a path of mercy.
Old English help gives our word, succor rendered to one in need.
Heb 13:6 carries the same confession into the new covenant, "The Lord is my helper."
usage: She raised her own Ebenezer after the long illness, confessing that hitherto the LORD had helped her.
In the worst of the trouble he clung to Psalm 46, that God is a very present help.
The help of God, not his own contriving, had carried the family through the lean years.

etymology: From Greek splanchna, the inward parts, used figuratively for tender compassion; the KJV renders it "bowels," the ancients seating the deepest affections in the viscera.
biblical_def: Bowels of mercy is the rich KJV idiom for the deepest, tenderest compassion, the pity that stirs in a man's inmost being toward the wretched and the needy. The Greek splanchna named the inward parts, and as the Hebrews seated affection in the heart and kidneys, so the Greeks located the strongest yearnings in the bowels; hence the apostle bids the saints, "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind" (Col 3:12). He pleads for unity by "any bowels and mercies" in Christ (Phil 2:1), and warns that he who shuts up his "bowels of compassion" from his needy brother has not the love of God dwelling in him (1 John 3:17). This is no shallow sentiment but a visceral, Christlike yearning, for it is written that Jesus, seeing the multitudes, was "moved with compassion" (the verb splanchnizomai), His very inward parts stirred toward the helpless. This dictionary confesses that the mercy God requires is not a cold duty but a warm, inward affection, planted by the Spirit, mirroring the tender compassion of Christ toward sinners and binding the saints in genuine love.
webster_summary: Bowels of mercy is the KJV idiom for tender compassion seated in the inward affections, rendering Greek splanchna. It names a visceral, Christlike pity toward the needy. The compassion of Christ was moved toward the wretched in just this way.
webster_full: BOWELS OF MERCY, noun phrase. The deepest and tenderest compassion, figuratively seated in the inward parts.
It renders the Greek splanchna, the viscera, used by the ancients as the seat of the strongest affections.
"Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind" (Col 3:12).
It requires a warm, inward pity toward the needy; it forbids the shutting up of compassion from a brother in want.
It mirrors the compassion of Christ, who was moved in His very inward parts toward the helpless multitudes.
scriptures: Col 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
Phil 2:1
If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels and mercies,
1 John 3:17
But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
Col 3:13
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
corruption_summary: There is little postmodern redefinition of the phrase itself, but the vivid KJV idiom is often dismissed as quaint and its visceral demand for compassion is softened to a tepid niceness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern readers stumble at the word "bowels" and hasten to translate it into the blander "heart" or "compassion," and in the smoothing the strength is lost. The idiom was meant to be visceral, naming a pity that grips a man in his inmost parts; to flatten it is to dull the edge of the apostle's command.

Recover the force of the figure: mercy that is felt in the gut, not merely conceded by the will. Such was the compassion of Christ, who saw the multitudes as sheep without a shepherd and was moved in His very bowels toward them. The saint is to put on the same tender affection, opening his inward parts toward his brother in need rather than shutting them up against him.
roots_summary: Bowels renders Greek splanchna, the inward parts, the ancient seat of the tenderest affections.
roots_lines: Greek splanchna, the viscera, was used figuratively for the seat of pity and affection.
The verb splanchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, describes Christ's yearning over the crowds.
The KJV "bowels" preserves the literal force the older English readers understood without flinching.
Col 3:12 lists "bowels of mercies" first among the graces the elect are to put on.
1 John 3:17 makes the shutting up of the bowels of compassion a test of the love of God within.
usage: He pleaded with them by the bowels of mercy in Christ to forgive the one who had wronged them.
Her bowels of compassion were stirred at the sight of the orphan, and she opened her home that day.
The apostle does not ask for cold charity but for bowels of mercy, a pity felt in the inmost parts.

etymology: From Greek ho aion ho mellon, the coming age (Eph 1:21); age from Latin aetas, an era; the consummated kingdom over against the present evil age.
biblical_def: The age to come is the great era of consummated salvation which Christ inaugurated by His death and resurrection and will perfect at His return, set in contrast to "this present evil world" from which He delivers His people. Scripture speaks of two ages: "Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come" (Eph 1:21). Christ promised His followers eternal life "in the world to come" (Mark 10:30), and the apostle says believers have already "tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come" (Heb 6:5). Here lies the great truth of the already and the not-yet: the powers of the coming age have broken into the present through Christ and His Spirit, so that the kingdom is truly inaugurated, yet its full glory awaits the second coming. Against an over-realized scheme that claims all the blessings now and denies the bodily resurrection still to come, and against the dispensational scheme that postpones the kingdom to a future earthly age severed from Christ's present reign, this dictionary confesses that the age to come is already begun in the risen Christ and will be consummated at His glorious appearing, when God shall be all in all.
webster_summary: The age to come is the consummated kingdom inaugurated by Christ's death and resurrection and perfected at His return. Its powers have already broken into the present age through the Spirit. It is the already and the not-yet, against both over-realized and dispensational errors.
webster_full: AGE TO COME, noun phrase. The era of consummated salvation, inaugurated by Christ and to be perfected at His return.
It stands over against this present evil age, from which Christ delivers His people.
"And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come" (Heb 6:5).
It requires that we live as those upon whom the ends of the world are come, in hope and holiness.
It is already begun in the risen Christ and not yet consummated until His glorious appearing.
scriptures: Mark 10:30
But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.
Eph 1:21
Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come:
Heb 6:5
And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come,
Heb 2:5
For unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come, whereof we speak.
corruption_summary: Two errors flank the truth: an over-realized eschatology that claims all the age's blessings now, and dispensationalism, which postpones the kingdom to a future earthly age severed from Christ's present reign.
corruption_paragraphs: Some claim the age to come so fully in the present that they deny a future bodily resurrection or expect heaven on earth by human effort, an over-realized hope that collapses the not-yet into the now. On the opposite hand, the dispensationalism born of Darby and Scofield in the nineteenth century tears the kingdom out of Christ's present reign and exiles it to a future earthly millennium for ethnic Israel, splitting redemptive history where Scripture joins it. Both schemes mishandle the two ages the Bible sets before us.

Recover the apostolic balance of the already and the not-yet. In the risen Christ the powers of the coming age have truly broken in; believers taste its firstfruits by the indwelling Spirit. Yet the consummation tarries until the King returns to raise the dead, judge the world, and make all things new. We live between the ages, citizens of the age to come who labor and wait amid this present evil world.
roots_summary: The phrase renders Greek ho aion ho mellon, the coming age, the consummation set over against the present age.
roots_lines: Greek aion, age, marks a span or era of redemptive history rather than mere endless time.
The participle mellon, coming or about to be, names the age still future yet breaking in.
The two-age scheme of ho aion houtos and ho aion ho mellon shapes apostolic eschatology.
Heb 6:5 speaks of tasting the dunameis, powers, of the age to come even now.
Latin aetas stands behind English age, an era or period of appointed time.
usage: He preached that the powers of the age to come had already broken into the present through the Spirit.
The dispensational scheme severed the kingdom from Christ's present reign and pushed the age to come into a future earthly era.
Living between the ages, the church tastes the firstfruits of the world to come and waits for its fulness.

etymology: From treasure, Latin thesaurus, a store of valuables; here the surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven, laid up where moth and rust do not corrupt.
biblical_def: The treasure of the kingdom is the surpassing, all-exceeding worth of the kingdom of heaven and of Christ its King, a worth so great that the man who finds it gladly parts with all he has to possess it. Our Lord commands, "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matt 6:19-20), and adds the searching word, "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Matt 6:21). He likens the kingdom to "treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field" (Matt 13:44), and again to "a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it" (Matt 13:45-46). The note in both parables is joy, not grudging sacrifice; the man counts all loss for the excellency of what he has found. This dictionary confesses that Christ and His kingdom are the pearl of great price, worth the forsaking of every earthly thing, and that the heart truly converted treasures Him above all and lays up its riches in heaven.
webster_summary: The treasure of the kingdom is the surpassing worth of Christ and His reign, laid up in heaven where it cannot perish. The parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl of great price teach that it is worth selling all to gain. The note is joy, not grudging sacrifice.
webster_full: TREASURE OF THE KINGDOM, noun phrase. The surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven and of Christ its King.
It is treasure laid up in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt nor thieves break through.
"Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field" (Matt 13:44).
It requires that a man count all things loss to gain it, and lay up his riches above; it forbids the hoarding of perishable wealth.
Its possession is joy, for the man sells all he has and buys the field with gladness.
scriptures: Matt 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Matt 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Matt 13:44
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
Matt 13:46
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
corruption_summary: The age inverts the parable, treating earthly wealth as the true treasure and the kingdom as one optional good among many, rather than the pearl worth selling all to gain.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel turns the treasure of the kingdom upside down, making earthly riches the proof of God's favor and the kingdom a means to worldly gain, when Christ commands the opposite, to lay up treasure in heaven and count earthly wealth as that which moth and rust corrupt. The wider materialism of the age simply forgets the kingdom altogether and lays up its all on earth, so that where its treasure is, there its heart is also, far from God.

Recover the joy of the parables. The man who finds the hidden treasure and the merchant who finds the pearl do not part with their goods in grudging duty but for joy, counting the kingdom worth infinitely more than all they forsake. So the converted heart treasures Christ above every earthly thing and lays up its riches where they can never perish.
roots_summary: Treasure comes from Greek thesauros, a store or storehouse, used by Christ for the imperishable riches of the kingdom.
roots_lines: Greek thesauros, a store of valuables, lies behind both the "treasure" of Matt 6 and Matt 13.
The phrase "pearl of great price" renders margarites polutimos, a pearl of surpassing worth.
The verb "selleth all" (polei panta) marks the total cost gladly paid for the kingdom.
Latin thesaurus and Old French tresor give the English treasure.
Matt 6:21 ties the location of one's treasure to the disposition of one's heart.
usage: He preached that Christ is the pearl of great price, the treasure of the kingdom worth selling all to gain.
She laid up her treasure in heaven, holding her earthly goods with a loose and grateful hand.
The prosperity teacher reversed the parable, making earthly wealth the treasure and the kingdom a means to it.

etymology: From Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized or possessed by a demon; possession from Latin possidere, to hold or occupy, here the seizing of a person by an evil spirit.
biblical_def: Demon possession is the real and dreadful bondage of a person to one or more evil spirits, who indwell, torment, and at times control the one possessed, until Christ or His authority drives them out. The Greek daimonizomai, rendered "possessed with devils," describes a true seizure of body and faculties, not mere illness or superstition. The Gospels record many such cases: the Gadarene held by a legion of unclean spirits (Mark 5), the two fierce men of the tombs whom none could pass by (Matt 8:28), and the damsel with a spirit of divination whom Paul delivered (Acts 16:16-18). In every case the demons are real persons, malignant and intelligent, subject wholly to the word of Christ, who casts them out with authority and power. Yet Scripture sets sober bounds: the apostolic age of attesting signs has closed, and the believer is not to chase sensational deliverances nor to credit every affliction to a demon. The cessationist temper holds both truths, the reality of the demonic and the sufficiency of Christ's finished triumph over the powers (Col 2:15). This dictionary confesses that evil spirits are real and dangerous, that Christ reigns sovereign over them all, and that the saint resists the devil by faith, the word, and prayer, not by spectacle.
webster_summary: Demon possession is the real bondage of a person to evil spirits who indwell and torment until Christ casts them out. The Gospels record true seizures, not mere illness, all subject to Christ's sovereign authority. A cessationist sobriety holds the demonic to be real while rejecting sensationalism.
webster_full: DEMON POSSESSION, noun. The real seizure and bondage of a person by one or more evil spirits.
It renders the Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, describing a true indwelling, not mere disease or superstition.
"And they that were possessed with devils came to him; and he cast out the spirits with his word" (cf. Matt 8:16).
It requires sober vigilance and reliance on Christ's authority; it forbids both denial of the demonic and sensational hunting after it.
It stands wholly under the dominion of Christ, who spoiled principalities and powers and triumphed over them openly.
scriptures: Mark 5:8
For he said unto him, Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit.
Matt 8:28
And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way.
Acts 16:18
And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour.
Col 2:15
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
corruption_summary: Two errors flank the truth: a rationalism that explains the demonic away as mere illness or myth, and a sensationalism that sees demons behind every affliction and trades on spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal and naturalistic readers dismiss the Gospel accounts as primitive misunderstandings of epilepsy or madness, denying the reality of evil spirits that Christ Himself addressed as persons. On the opposite hand, much charismatic and continuationist practice runs to the other extreme, attributing every sin, sickness, and sorrow to a demon and staging dramatic deliverances as a kind of theater. Both dishonor the plain teaching of Scripture, the one by unbelief, the other by excess.

Recover the cessationist sobriety that takes the demonic seriously yet soberly. Evil spirits are real, malignant, and intelligent, but they are wholly subject to Christ, who spoiled the principalities and powers at the cross. The believer is not left to spectacle but is armed with the whole armor of God, resisting the devil by faith, the word, and prayer, assured that greater is He that is in us than he that is in the world.
roots_summary: The word renders Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, the seizing of a person by an unclean spirit.
roots_lines: Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, is the verb the Gospels use for those possessed with devils.
Greek daimonion, demon, names the evil spirit itself, a fallen and malignant person.
The phrase pneuma akatharton, unclean spirit, is used interchangeably in Mark 5.
Latin possidere, to hold or occupy, gives the English possession, the spirit's seizing of its victim.
Col 2:15 shows the demonic powers spoiled and openly triumphed over by Christ at the cross.
usage: He affirmed the reality of demon possession in the Gospels without crediting every illness to a demon.
The unclean spirits obeyed Christ's word at once, proof of His sovereign authority over the demonic.
Cessationist sobriety guards the church from both denying the demonic and chasing sensational deliverances.

etymology: From Gadarene, of the region of Gadara east of Galilee; demoniac from Greek daimonizomenos, one possessed by demons.
biblical_def: The Gadarene demoniac is the man, recorded chiefly in Mark 5:1-20 (with Matt 8 and Luke 8), who dwelt among the tombs in the country of the Gadarenes, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits and so fierce that no chains could bind him. He had "his dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains" (Mark 5:3), and night and day he cried and cut himself with stones. When Jesus came, the unclean spirit, asked his name, answered, "My name is Legion: for we are many" (Mark 5:9), and the demons besought leave to enter a herd of swine, whereupon "the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea" and perished (Mark 5:13). The men of the country came and found him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15), a living monument of Christ's power to deliver. The Lord then sent him home to publish how great things God had done for him. The accounts speak of Gadara and of Gergesa, neighboring places of the same region named with differing precision, no contradiction but the ordinary breadth of a district's name. This dictionary confesses the narrative as sober history, displaying Christ's absolute sovereignty over the powers of darkness and His mercy in restoring a man whom the demons had wholly undone.
webster_summary: The Gadarene demoniac is the man of Mark 5 who dwelt among the tombs, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits whom Christ cast into the swine. Afterward he sat clothed and in his right mind, a monument of deliverance. The Gadara and Gergesa references name the same region with differing precision.
webster_full: GADARENE DEMONIAC, noun. The man of the Gadarene country, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits, whom Christ delivered.
He dwelt among the tombs, untamable and self-wounding, until the Lord cast the demons into the swine.
"And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15).
His deliverance displays Christ's sovereign authority over the powers and His mercy toward the wretched.
Restored, he was sent home to publish how great things the Lord had done for him.
scriptures: Mark 5:9
And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many.
Mark 5:13

And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
Mark 5:15
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
Luke 8:35

Then they went out to see what was done; and came to Jesus, and found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
corruption_summary: Critics seize on the Gadara and Gergesa references to allege a geographical contradiction, and naturalists explain the possession away as mere madness rather than real demonic bondage.
corruption_paragraphs: Skeptics point to the naming of Gadara, Gergesa, and the Gerasenes across the Gospel manuscripts and parallels as proof of error, but this is no contradiction. Gadara was a chief city of the district, Gergesa a nearer town by the lakeshore, and the region could be named by either with differing precision, much as one might place an event near a county or near its principal town. The Evangelists report the same true event from the same region. Likewise the naturalist who reduces the man's state to insanity must explain away the intelligent speech of the demons, their bargaining, and their entrance into the swine.

Recover the narrative as sober history and rich gospel. Here is a man wholly mastered by a legion of spirits, beyond all human help, whom Christ restores with a word, leaving him clothed and in his right mind at the Master's feet. The account magnifies the Lord's absolute dominion over the powers of darkness and His tender mercy toward the most ruined of sinners, and ends with the delivered man sent home to testify.
roots_summary: Gadarene names the region of Gadara, and demoniac renders Greek daimonizomenos, one possessed by demons.
roots_lines: Gadarene derives from Gadara, a chief city of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee.
Gergesa, the reading in some accounts, names a nearer lakeside town within the same district.
Greek daimonizomenos, demonized, supplies the English demoniac, one held by evil spirits.
Legion renders the Latin legio, a Roman unit of thousands, marking the multitude of the demons.
The phrase "in his right mind" (sophronounta) names the soundness Christ restored to the man.
usage: The Gadarene demoniac, once untamable among the tombs, sat clothed and in his right mind at Christ's feet.
He showed that the Gadara and Gergesa references name one region, not a contradiction in the Gospels.
Legion cast into the swine displays Christ's utter dominion over the demonic powers.
